subject: Business Models
title: Groupon: The Daily Deal Death Spiral
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Groupon: The Daily Deal Death Spiral.

hook.text: Groupon rejected Google's $6 billion acquisition offer in 2010. It's now worth under $500 million.

buildup.text: Groupon sold daily deals: 50% off local businesses. It kept 50% of the deal revenue as commission.

discovery.text: Groupon attracted bargain hunters, not loyal customers. Businesses got one-time visitors who never paid full price.

twist.text: Local businesses lost money on Groupon deals hoping for repeat customers. Most never broke even on the promotion.

climax.text: Groupon damaged the businesses it claimed to help. When merchants stopped participating, the deal flow dried up.

punchline.text: Rejected $6B. Now under $500M. It trained customers to never pay full price.

quiz.question: Why did local businesses stop using Groupon?
options: Deals attracted one-time bargain hunters who never returned

details.summary: Groupon pioneered daily deals with explosive growth, reaching the fastest IPO in history. But merchants found that deal customers rarely returned at full price, and Groupon's model attracted bargain hunters rather than loyal new customers. Revenue collapsed as merchants stopped participating.
details.whyItMatters: Groupon showed that a business model serving neither side well eventually collapses. Merchants lost money on deals. Customers became trained to wait for discounts..
takeaways: Deal customers rarely returned at full price, providing no lasting value for merchants
Groupon grew to IPO by sacrificing merchant satisfaction for volume
The daily deal model trained customers to expect deep discounts permanently

faq.question: Why did merchants stop using Groupon?
faq.answer: Merchants typically offered 50 percent discounts and gave Groupon half the sale price, receiving only 25 cents per dollar of normal revenue. Deal-seeking customers rarely returned at full price. Many merchants lost money on every Groupon sale and saw no long-term customer acquisition benefit.

faq.question: What could Groupon have done differently to sustain its business?
faq.answer: Focus on customer retention tools for merchants rather than one-time deals. Build loyalty programs, repeat visit incentives, and CRM tools. Target customers likely to return rather than pure deal seekers. Charge merchants less to make the economics work for both sides.
